tip: 'a' (and) aspirate-mutates the very next word if it starts p, t or c: 'papur' becomes 'a phapur'.
'gad i fi' plus a verb = let me. The verb softens after it, so 'gweld' becomes 'weld' in 'gad i fi weld'.
'dal ati i' plus a verb means keep on doing something. 'dal ati i freuddwydio' = keep on dreaming.
South Welsh shows having something with 'gyda'. 'mae stumog tost gyda fi' is literally a stomach ache is with me = I have one.
The word 'i' (to) changes shape by person. To her is 'iddi', as in 'rhoddodd e'r anrheg iddi hi'.
You ask a question to a person in Welsh, using 'gofyn i'. 'gofynnodd e gwestiwn i mi' = he asked me a question.
To bring is 'dod â', literally to come with. 'daethon ni â blodau' = we brought flowers.
The feminine 'ei' (her) adds an h before a word starting with a vowel. Her umbrella becomes 'ei hymbarél'.
Before someone does something uses 'cyn i' plus that person. 'cyn iddyn nhw gyrraedd' = before they arrive.
A feminine noun usually softens after 'y' (the). 'cadair' becomes 'gadair', so on the chair is 'ar y gadair'.
Go for a walk is the set phrase 'mynd am dro', literally to go for a turn.
Place names usually soften after 'i' (to). 'Bangor' becomes 'Fangor', so to Bangor is 'i Fangor'.
The ending '-wyd' makes an action impersonal, with no named doer. 'penderfynwyd' means it was decided.
The word 'dan' (under) softens the next word. 'pwysau' becomes 'bwysau', so under pressure is 'dan bwysau'.
To report that something is the case, use 'fod'. 'fod y ffordd ar gau' = that the road is closed.
After 'o' (of), the noun softens. 'llyfrau' becomes 'lyfrau', so a lot of books is 'llawer o lyfrau'.
Linking 'yn' usually softens the word after it. 'cawl' becomes 'gawl', so is a soup is 'yn gawl'.
To care for someone is 'gofalu am', using 'am' (for). 'gofalu am y fam' = caring for the mother.
To look forward to something is 'edrych ymlaen at', using 'at'. 'edrych ymlaen at y tymor' = looking forward to the term.
'hen' (old) goes before its noun and softens it. 'tŷ' becomes 'dŷ', so old house is 'hen dŷ'.
'hoffwn i' means I would like, a polite way to ask for things. 'hoffwn i gael' = I would like to have.
The word 'am' (about, for) changes shape by person. For it is 'amdano', as in 'i fod yn ddiolchgar amdano' = to be grateful for it.
After 'yn' (in), some words take a nasal mutation, and 'yn' becomes 'ym'. 'Patagonia' becomes 'ym Mhatagonia'.
Put a word first for emphasis, then 'y' and the verb. 'rygbi y mae Cymru'n enwog amdano' = it's rugby that Wales is famous for.
'ar' triggers soft mutation, so 'coll' (loss) becomes 'goll': 'ar goll' = lost.
Listen to is 'gwrando ar', never 'gwrando i' or 'gwrando am'. 'gwrandewais i ar gerddoriaeth' means I listened to music.
'gyda' causes aspirate mutation, turning p to ph: 'pob' becomes 'phob', as in 'gyda phob dymuniad da'.
The object of a short-form verb softens: 'tŷ' becomes 'dŷ' after 'prynodd e' (he bought). Hence 'prynodd e dŷ newydd'.
The '-wch' ending makes a formal or plural command: 'parhewch' means continue, spoken politely or to several people.
Welsh has no verb meaning to have. Possession is 'mae gen i' (there is with me): 'mae gen i gydweithwyr da' = I have good colleagues.
